sourceNotes: Seeded from ACT roleplay performance indicators and finance cluster exam data.
Drawn in three tiers: ACT event flavor first, then this event's own instructional areas woven with the rest of the finance cluster exam blueprint.
Terms are scoped for future vocab-card, quiz, and event-filter UI use.

terms.definition: The direct cost of inventory or materials sold to customers.
terms.whyItMatters: COGS affects gross profit and pricing decisions.

terms.definition: Assets equal liabilities plus owner's equity — the identity every transaction must leave intact, which is why a single-sided entry is always an error.
terms.whyItMatters: Accounting Applications items give two of the three figures and ask for the third, and the same identity is what a competitor uses to prove a balance sheet balances.

terms.definition: A system recording every transaction in at least two accounts so that total debits equal total credits, which is what makes an out-of-balance ledger detectable.
terms.whyItMatters: An ACT roleplay asking a competitor to explain why the books will not balance expects this rule, not a search for a missing receipt.

terms.definition: The left side of an account, which increases assets and expenses but decreases liabilities, equity and revenue — direction depends on the account type, not on whether money came in.
terms.whyItMatters: Journalizing items on the accounting exam are lost by assuming a debit always means an increase, which is only true for half the account types.

terms.definition: The right side of an account, which increases liabilities, equity and revenue but decreases assets and expenses — the mirror of a debit, and unrelated to a credit card.
terms.whyItMatters: Recording a cash sale on the exam requires debiting cash and crediting revenue; reversing the pair is the single most common journalizing error.

terms.definition: A two-column sketch of one account with debits on the left and credits on the right, used to work out an entry before it is journalized.
terms.whyItMatters: Competitors use these to reason through a multi-account transaction under exam time pressure rather than journalizing straight from memory.

terms.definition: A period-end entry recording revenue earned or expense incurred that no cash transaction has yet captured, such as accrued wages or expired prepaid insurance.
terms.whyItMatters: Exam items ask what happens if one is skipped: the statements misstate both net income and the balance sheet for that period.

terms.definition: A period-end entry zeroing revenue, expense and drawing accounts into equity so the next period starts fresh, while asset and liability balances carry forward.
terms.whyItMatters: Distinguishing which accounts close from which carry over is a recurring accounting-exam item and the reason temporary and permanent accounts are named that way.

terms.definition: Expenses are recorded in the same period as the revenue they helped produce, not in the period they were paid, which is what forces period-end adjustments.
terms.whyItMatters: It is the reason an ACT scenario records December commissions against December sales even though the checks clear in January.

terms.definition: Revenue is recorded when the good or service is delivered, not when the order is signed or the cash arrives, so a deposit on undelivered work is a liability.
terms.whyItMatters: A client in an accounting roleplay who wants to book a prepayment as this month's sales is asking for something this rule forbids.

terms.definition: Financial statements are prepared on the premise the business will keep operating, which is why assets are carried at cost rather than at what they would fetch in a liquidation.
terms.whyItMatters: It explains an exam answer competitors find odd — that a balance sheet does not report what a company is worth if sold today.

terms.definition: Cost minus salvage value divided by useful life, producing the same expense every year of an asset's life.
terms.whyItMatters: Accounting exam items hand over a purchase price, a salvage value and a life expectancy and expect the annual figure computed, not estimated.

terms.definition: An accelerated method applying a fixed rate to the asset's remaining book value, so expense is largest in year one and falls every year after.
terms.whyItMatters: Choosing between this and the straight-line method changes reported net income early in an asset's life, which is exactly what an exam item tests.

terms.definition: An inventory costing method assuming the oldest units sell first, which in a period of rising prices leaves newer, costlier units on the balance sheet and reports higher profit.
terms.whyItMatters: Accounting items give a purchase history and ask for ending inventory; the costing method chosen changes the answer even though the physical goods are identical.

terms.definition: An inventory costing method assuming the newest units sell first, which under rising prices charges the higher costs against revenue and reports lower profit and lower tax.
terms.whyItMatters: The tax consequence is the point of the exam item: two firms with identical inventory report different net income purely on this choice.

terms.definition: Costing inventory at total cost of goods available divided by total units available, so every unit carries the same average cost regardless of when it was bought.
terms.whyItMatters: It is the third answer choice on every inventory-costing item, and it lands between the FIFO and LIFO figures under rising prices.

terms.definition: Recording revenue and expenses only when cash moves, which is simpler than the accrual basis but reports a month's profit in whichever period the payment happens to land.
terms.whyItMatters: An ACT roleplay advising a small client on which basis to use rests on this distortion, and most businesses above a size threshold may not use it.

terms.definition: An account deliberately carrying a balance opposite its partner — accumulated depreciation against an asset, sales returns against revenue — so the original figure stays visible alongside the reduction.
terms.whyItMatters: It answers the exam item asking why equipment still shows its full purchase price years after it was bought.

terms.definition: A contra-asset estimate of receivables that will never be collected, recorded in the period of the sale rather than when a specific customer's account is finally written off.
terms.whyItMatters: Accounting items test the timing: estimating bad debt up front is what keeps the expense in the same period as the revenue it came from.

terms.definition: The common rule set governing how U.S. financial statements are prepared, which is what lets an outside reader compare two companies' books at all.
terms.whyItMatters: An ACT roleplay where a client wants to record something a convenient way is answered by whether these rules permit it, not by whether it looks reasonable.

terms.definition: Cash collected before the work is delivered, recorded as a liability rather than income until the obligation is filled.
terms.whyItMatters: Accounting items give a customer deposit and ask where it lands on the statements; calling it revenue overstates income for the period.

terms.definition: Cash paid ahead for a future benefit — insurance or rent — carried as an asset and expensed a period at a time as it is used up.
terms.whyItMatters: It is the standard period-end adjustment on the accounting exam: the payment happened once, the expense belongs to several months.

terms.definition: An asset's original cost minus accumulated depreciation, which is what the ledger reports and rarely what the asset would sell for.
terms.whyItMatters: Items ask for the reported value of equipment after three years, and the answer requires subtracting the accumulated total, not one year's depreciation.

terms.definition: Net credit sales divided by average receivables, counting how many times a year a business collects what customers owe it.
terms.whyItMatters: A falling figure in an accounting scenario is the early warning that credit customers are paying slower, before any account goes bad.

terms.definition: Updating inventory and cost of goods sold at every sale, so the balance is known continuously — unlike a periodic system, which learns it only from a physical count.
terms.whyItMatters: Which system a business runs decides whether an ACT scenario can state cost of goods sold mid-period or has to wait for the count.

terms.definition: The procedures protecting assets and records — separating who authorizes, who records and who holds the cash — so no one person can both commit and conceal an error.
terms.whyItMatters: An ACT roleplay asking how a small business prevents theft expects this separation of duties, not stricter hiring.

terms.definition: Paying a loan off through fixed installments split between interest and principal, with the interest share largest at the start and shrinking every payment.
terms.whyItMatters: Exam items ask why an early mortgage payment barely reduces the balance; the amortization split is the reason, not a fee.

terms.definition: Normalization's opening stage: every column holds one indivisible value and no table repeats a group of columns across a single row (no phone1, phone2, phone3). It removes repeating groups and nothing else — a partial dependency on part of a composite key survives it, and a transitive dependency survives both it and the second stage.
terms.whyItMatters: A database item hands the competitor a customer table with three comma-packed phone columns and asks which normal form it breaks; the answer is the first, and answering the third throws the point away.

terms.definition: Stretch of the calendar when insiders may not trade their own company's stock, typically closing two to four weeks before quarter-end and reopening one to two full trading days after earnings are released. A Rule 10b5-1 plan is the only clean way around it: trades are pre-scheduled and, under the 2023 amendments, cannot begin for at least 90 days.
terms.whyItMatters: A corporate-finance roleplay in which an employee wants to sell vested shares the week before an earnings release is answered by the window, not by intent.

terms.definition: A document a seller issues to request payment for goods or services provided.
terms.whyItMatters: Invoices drive accounts-receivable timing and payment terms.

terms.definition: Current assets divided by current liabilities, the standard test of whether a business can cover what it owes within the next twelve months.
terms.whyItMatters: Finance exam items hand over a balance sheet and ask whether the firm can meet short-term obligations; a ratio under 1.0 is the answer that says no.

terms.definition: The pretrial phase in which each side must turn over relevant evidence through interrogatories, requests for production, depositions and requests for admission — which is why most business disputes settle once the documents surface. It also creates a duty to preserve records the moment litigation is reasonably anticipated, so routine deletion schedules have to be suspended under a litigation hold.
terms.whyItMatters: Legal-procedure roleplays about a document-retention policy hinge on the litigation hold this phase triggers.

terms.definition: A structured request that filters and retrieves specific information from a database.
terms.whyItMatters: Querying lets competitors pull exactly the data they need instead of sifting everything.

terms.definition: Flat daily travel allowance that substitutes for itemized receipts — the federal standard for the continental U.S. runs near $110 for lodging plus $68 for meals and incidentals, with the first and last travel days paid at 75% of the meal portion. Anything paid above the published rate becomes taxable wages to the traveler.
terms.whyItMatters: A hospitality or sales roleplay budgeting a three-day trip needs the arithmetic: two full days at the meal rate plus two partial days at three quarters of it.

terms.definition: Current assets minus current liabilities — a measure of short-term financial health.
terms.whyItMatters: Working capital shows whether a business can cover immediate obligations.

terms.definition: Current assets minus inventory, divided by current liabilities — the stricter liquidity test, because inventory may not convert to cash in time to pay a bill.
terms.whyItMatters: A retailer with a healthy current ratio and a weak quick ratio is the classic exam case, and the difference is inventory the business cannot sell fast.

terms.definition: The stage requiring every non-key column to depend on the whole composite key rather than on one piece of it — a table keyed on (order_id, product_id) that also stores the customer's name breaks it, because the name follows order_id alone. It does nothing whatever when the key is a single column, since a one-column key has no part to depend on.
terms.whyItMatters: Given a table already in first normal form, an exam item asks what still has to be split out; only the partial-dependency test tells the competitor which columns move to a new table.

terms.definition: Estimates U.S. grade level from letters rather than syllables: 0.0588 x (letters per 100 words) - 0.296 x (sentences per 100 words) - 15.8. Counting characters is the point - a syllable count needs a pronunciation dictionary and a character count does not - which is why word processors and web tools can score a document automatically, and why it rates dense technical prose full of short-but-long-lettered words harder than Flesch-Kincaid does.
terms.whyItMatters: An exam item asking which readability check a company can run inside its own email platform with no extra software is testing the characters-versus-syllables distinction.

terms.definition: Dollar ceiling below which accepting a business courtesy is not treated as influence — federal ethics rules cap it at $20 per occasion and $50 per source per year, and many corporate policies copy those figures. Above the line the item must be refused, returned, or reported, and splitting one gift across two occasions is itself the violation.
terms.whyItMatters: A purchasing roleplay where a vendor sends playoff tickets is scored on whether the competitor applies the stated dollar limit and the reporting step.

terms.definition: Recording revenue or expense when it is incurred, not when cash changes hands.
terms.whyItMatters: Accrual accounting reveals true profitability beyond the cash view.

terms.definition: A tax structure whose rate rises as income rises, taxing each band of income at its own rate — the opposite of a regressive tax that takes a larger share from lower earners.
terms.whyItMatters: Tax-structure questions ask competitors to classify income tax, sales tax and payroll tax, and sales tax is regressive despite its single rate.

terms.definition: An arbitrary system-generated identifier — normally an auto-incrementing integer — carrying no business meaning, chosen over a natural identifier such as an email address or a part number precisely because the business can change the natural value. When a supplier renumbers all 4,000 of its parts, rows keyed on the part number break every reference pointing at them; rows keyed on the integer do not move at all.
terms.whyItMatters: A roleplay on migrating a supplier catalog asks which column should identify a part; picking the meaningful one is what forces the rework the judge is listening for.

terms.definition: Post-employment restriction barring a departing worker from joining a competitor for a stated period and geography, commonly 6 to 12 months. Enforceability is a state question — California voids them outright and several states exempt hourly workers below a wage threshold — and a court will usually narrow an unreasonable radius rather than rewrite the deal.
terms.whyItMatters: A roleplay advising an employee who has an offer from a rival turns on this clause's scope and on whether the state will enforce it at all.

terms.definition: Any gap between what the customer expected and what was delivered, including delivery that met every internal specification — a technically perfect order arriving after a promised time has failed. A defect is a measurable breach of a standard the company set, so every defect is a failure while many failures pass every internal check, which is why complaint data can never be replaced by quality-control data.
terms.whyItMatters: A roleplay where the operation insists nothing went wrong is won by naming this distinction before proposing the remedy.

terms.definition: Money a business owes to suppliers for goods or services already received.
terms.whyItMatters: Payables shape the cash position competitors must manage.

terms.definition: Total liabilities divided by owner's equity, showing how much of the business is financed by lenders rather than owners and how exposed it is to a downturn.
terms.whyItMatters: Financing scenarios ask whether a firm can take on another loan, and a high ratio is the reason a lender says no.

terms.definition: The enforced rule that every foreign-key value must match a primary-key value that actually exists in the parent table; with it turned on the engine rejects an orphan child row outright, and a delete of a parent must either cascade to its children or be refused, never silently leave them stranded.
terms.whyItMatters: A roleplay about a corrupted customer database usually ends with the judge asking what stops a deleted account from leaving unreachable orders behind, and this constraint is the answer.

terms.definition: Reimbursement arrangement that keeps expense payments out of taxable wages, valid only when the expense has a business connection, is substantiated with receipts within 60 days, and any excess advance is returned within 120 days. Miss any one of the three and the arrangement is non-accountable, so every reimbursed dollar is added to the W-2 and taxed as pay.
terms.whyItMatters: An exam item on a sales rep who never turns in travel receipts is really asking why the reimbursement showed up as taxable income.

terms.definition: A list of all ledger accounts and balances used to check that debits equal credits.
terms.whyItMatters: Trial balances verify the accuracy of financial records in case work.

terms.definition: Fraction of checkable deposits a bank is barred from lending — mandated reserves ÷ deposits. At 10%, a $1,000 deposit locks up $100 and frees $900, and the ceiling on deposit creation is 1 ÷ 0.10 = 10; cutting the ratio to 5% doubles that ceiling without the central bank buying a single security.
terms.whyItMatters: Interest-rate-fluctuation items ask how a change in this one fraction moves the amount of money in circulation, and the answer is the reciprocal.

terms.definition: The payroll deduction funding Social Security and Medicare, taken at a fixed percentage of wages and matched dollar for dollar by the employer.
terms.whyItMatters: Pay-stub interpretation items ask why gross pay minus income tax still does not equal take-home pay, and FICA is the missing line.

terms.definition: Keeps every row of the first table and fills the second table's columns with NULL wherever no match exists — those same 120 order-less customers come back, so COUNT(*) returns 500 while COUNT(order_id) returns 380, and the 120-row gap between the two counts is precisely the set that had no match.
terms.whyItMatters: Asked to list customers who bought nothing this quarter, the competitor has to name this join and then filter on the NULL — the inner join cannot produce that list at all.

terms.definition: Withholding certificate an employee files so the employer deducts the right federal income tax; the 2020 redesign dropped allowances for a five-step worksheet stated in dollars, including $2,000 per qualifying child. It is not Form I-9, which proves work authorization within three business days of hire, nor Form W-9, which an independent contractor files instead.
terms.whyItMatters: A first-day onboarding roleplay is scored on knowing which of the three forms does what, since a competitor who names the wrong one has the new hire unpaid or unauthorized.

terms.definition: The dollar gap between inventory valued under FIFO and the same inventory valued under LIFO — FIFO inventory minus LIFO inventory — disclosed in the notes so a reader can restate a LIFO firm's inventory and cost of goods sold onto a FIFO basis before comparing it with anyone else.
terms.whyItMatters: Finance exam items hand you a footnote figure and ask you to compare two competitors' inventory when one uses LIFO and one uses FIFO; the comparison means nothing until the reserve is added back.

terms.definition: Net income divided by owner's equity, measuring profit generated per dollar the owners have invested rather than per dollar of sales.
terms.whyItMatters: Exam items compare two firms with equal profits and different equity bases; the one earning more per invested dollar wins.

terms.definition: Motivational push-back triggered by a perceived restriction on a freedom, which makes the restricted option more attractive rather than less -- the boomerang result seen when warning labels raise interest and mandates raise resistance. It is distinguishable from ordinary disagreement because the target's preference shifts even when they had no prior stake in the option, so the intensity is about the constraint, not the content.
terms.whyItMatters: Leading-change roleplays hinge on this: announcing a mandatory new system produces opposition from people who never used the old one, and the scoring move is to restore a real choice -- rollout timing, pilot team, tool configuration -- rather than to re-explain the rationale.

terms.definition: Filters whole groups after aggregation, where WHERE filters individual rows before it: 'WHERE amount > 100' throws out small orders and then sums what remains, while 'HAVING SUM(amount) > 100' keeps every order and throws out customers whose total falls short. Run on the same table, the two return different customer lists.
terms.whyItMatters: A query item asks for customers whose yearly spend tops a threshold; putting the test in the WHERE clause returns the wrong set even though the query runs without error.

terms.definition: Narrower post-employment restriction that lets a departing worker take any job but forbids contacting the former employer's customers or recruiting its staff, usually for 12 to 24 months. Because it limits whom you may approach rather than where you may work, courts enforce it in states that will not enforce a non-compete at all.
terms.whyItMatters: A sales-management roleplay about a rep who leaves and calls his old book of business is decided by this clause, not by the broader competition ban.

terms.definition: Money owed to a business by customers for goods or services already delivered.
terms.whyItMatters: Receivables affect cash flow timing and collection decisions.

terms.definition: Net income available to common shareholders divided by shares outstanding, the per-share figure that lets companies of different sizes be compared.
terms.whyItMatters: Investment scenarios quote it as the headline number, and a competitor is expected to know a buyback raises it without any change in profit.

terms.definition: A table containing little more than two foreign keys, plus any attribute that belongs to the pairing itself, which converts a single many-to-many relationship into two one-to-many relationships; without it a students-and-courses design has nowhere legal to record that one pair, since neither side's table has room for many values.
terms.whyItMatters: Database-design questions that describe products appearing in many orders and orders holding many products are testing whether you add this third table rather than repeating columns.

terms.definition: The employment eligibility verification record required of every U.S. employer by the Immigration Reform and Control Act: the employee completes Section 1 no later than the first day of work for pay, and the employer examines original documents and completes Section 2 within three business days of that start. The form is retained three years after hire or one year after termination, whichever is later, and is kept apart from the personnel file.
terms.whyItMatters: An onboarding roleplay that lists paperwork must place this inside the three-business-day window, a deadline competitors routinely confuse with the first payroll run.

terms.definition: State or city rule requiring an employer to publish a good-faith salary range inside the job posting itself, as Colorado's Equal Pay for Equal Work Act and New York City's Local Law 32 do. It attacks the gap at the offer stage, whereas the Equal Pay Act of 1963 works after the fact by requiring equal pay for substantially equal work.
terms.whyItMatters: A roleplay preparing a competitor to negotiate an offer changes completely when the posted range is public, because the anchor is set before the conversation.

terms.definition: A write-down rule under ASC 330: inventory carried at historical cost must be reduced to replacement cost when that is lower, but never above net realizable value — selling price minus completion and disposal costs — nor below that ceiling minus a normal profit margin.
terms.whyItMatters: Roleplay judges ask what to do about obsolete stock still on the books at full cost; the answer is the mandatory write-down and the loss it forces onto this period's income statement.

terms.definition: A retirement account whose contributions escape tax now and whose withdrawals are taxed later, trading a deduction today for taxable income in retirement.
terms.whyItMatters: Retirement-planning roleplays turn on when the client wants the tax bill, which is the whole traditional-versus-Roth decision.

terms.definition: The balanced tree structure behind most database indexes: a lookup descends a few levels instead of reading every row, costing about log2(n) page reads — roughly 20 steps in a 1,000,000-row table where a full scan touches all 1,000,000. Doubling the table adds a single step, so an index worth little at 10,000 rows is worth enormously more at 10,000,000.
terms.whyItMatters: Asked why a customer lookup that was instant last year now takes 30 seconds, the competitor has to contrast logarithmic index cost with linear scan cost rather than blame the server.

terms.definition: Employment clause transferring to the employer any invention conceived during the job, reaching further than copyright's work-made-for-hire rule because it also captures patents. Statutes such as California Labor Code section 2870 carve out inventions developed entirely on the worker's own time, without company equipment or trade secrets, and unrelated to the employer's business.
terms.whyItMatters: An entrepreneurship roleplay about a side project built after hours is scored on whether the competitor can state the carve-out's three conditions.

terms.definition: The share and cost lead a pioneer can lock in through buyer switching costs, scarce shelf space or spectrum, and a learning-curve cost position — but Golder and Tellis found market pioneers failed roughly 47% of the time and held about 10% share on average, while the fast follower entering after the category's standard settles skips the cost of educating the market and buys the pioneer's proof of demand for free.
terms.whyItMatters: Roleplays about racing a competitor to launch expect both sides argued with evidence; asserting that being first always wins is the answer the data contradicts.

terms.definition: An estimate of ending inventory made without a physical count: multiply net sales by the historical gross-profit percentage to approximate cost of goods sold, then subtract that from the cost of goods available for sale.
terms.whyItMatters: Insurance-claim and interim-statement questions give you sales figures and a prior-year margin but no count, and this is the only route to an inventory number a judge will accept.

terms.definition: Share price divided by earnings per share, the number of dollars investors pay for each dollar of annual profit — a rough gauge of how much growth is priced in.
terms.whyItMatters: Advising a client on whether a stock looks expensive in an investing roleplay turns on this multiple, not on the share price alone.

terms.definition: The share of a table's rows a filter matches, taken as matching rows over total rows: 200 hits in 100,000 rows is 0.2% and the optimizer uses the index, while a filter matching 40,000 of those rows is unselective and a full scan wins, because chasing 40,000 index pointers back into the table costs more than reading the table once.
terms.whyItMatters: An item asks why adding an index on a two-value status column changed nothing; the fraction of rows matched, not the presence of the index, decides it.

terms.definition: Paid notice period during which a resigning employee stays on payroll but is kept away from the office, from clients and from starting at a competitor, commonly one to six months. It is enforceable in places that void a bare non-compete precisely because the employer keeps paying — the restraint is bought rather than merely imposed.
terms.whyItMatters: A roleplay advising a senior manager on a competitor's offer must separate this paid restriction from an unpaid non-compete, because only one keeps income flowing.

terms.definition: The difference between a budgeted amount and the actual amount spent or earned.
terms.whyItMatters: Variances flag where a plan and reality diverge, prompting corrective action.

terms.definition: A Pareto split of stock by annual dollar usage: roughly the top 20 percent of items carrying about 80 percent of the value are class A and get tight control and frequent counts, class B moderate control, class C the low-value bulk that is managed loosely with large buffers.
terms.whyItMatters: Asked how a warehouse manager should spend limited counting and control effort, the accepted answer is to classify by dollar usage and concentrate on class A rather than treat every item alike.

terms.definition: A retirement account funded with money already taxed, whose qualified withdrawals — contributions and growth alike — come out tax-free.
terms.whyItMatters: Advising a young client in a retirement roleplay usually points here, because decades of growth escape tax when the current bracket is low.

terms.definition: Deliberately putting back the duplicated columns that normalization removed, trading write cost and update anomalies for read speed: one wide table answers a report with zero joins, but a customer who changes her surname must now be rewritten in every row that copied it, and any row missed is a silent contradiction.
terms.whyItMatters: A reporting-performance roleplay asks why the analytics table repeats the region name in a million rows; the defensible answer is the read-versus-write trade-off, not sloppy design.

terms.definition: Department of Labor-registered training program pairing paid on-the-job hours — about 2,000 a year under a journey-worker mentor — with at least 144 hours of related classroom instruction and scheduled wage increases as each skill is certified. An internship carries no registered hour floor, no mentor requirement and no guaranteed wage progression.
terms.whyItMatters: A roleplay on ways to gain real work experience is scored on naming the structured, paid, credentialed route rather than only the summer internship.

terms.definition: Delivery terms placing title and risk of loss with the buyer the moment a carrier takes the goods, so the buyer adds the freight to inventory cost and reports goods still in transit at period end — the mirror of FOB destination, where the seller keeps both title and freight until delivery.
terms.whyItMatters: Cutoff questions ask which company reports a shipment sitting on a truck on December 31, and the answer turns entirely on which of the two terms the invoice names.

terms.definition: Annual dividends per share divided by share price, stating income return as a percentage so a dividend stock can be compared against a savings rate.
terms.whyItMatters: A client asking for income rather than growth in a retirement roleplay is asking about this figure, which moves whenever the share price moves.

terms.definition: The measured pattern in which unit cost falls by a constant percentage each time cumulative output doubles — an 80% curve means the 200th unit costs 80% of the 100th — so the advantage belongs to accumulated experience, not to current period volume as in economies of scale.
terms.whyItMatters: Exam items give a starting unit cost and a curve percentage and expect the cost after a doubling, so the arithmetic has to be known and not just the idea that practice helps.

terms.definition: Splitting one table's rows horizontally across several servers by a key, so four servers each carry about 25% of the rows and the system gains write capacity and room. Replication does the opposite — it copies 100% of the rows onto every server, buying read capacity and failover but not one byte of extra space.
terms.whyItMatters: A roleplay on a database that has outgrown its server asks which approach fixes it; recommending more copies of a table that no longer fits is the trap the judge is watching for.

terms.definition: Employment term routing disputes to a private arbitrator instead of a court, waiving a jury and usually class treatment; the Federal Arbitration Act makes it binding and the award is nearly unappealable on the merits. The 2022 Ending Forced Arbitration Act carves out sexual assault and harassment claims, which an employee may still take to court.
terms.whyItMatters: A roleplay walking a new hire through an offer packet has to flag what this clause gives up, since signing happens on day one and matters years later.

terms.definition: A bad-debt estimate built from a schedule that sorts every customer balance by days past due and applies a rising uncollectible rate to each bucket, targeting the ENDING allowance balance — unlike the percentage-of-sales approach, which computes the period's expense straight from revenue and ignores whatever already sits in the allowance.
terms.whyItMatters: A finance exam gives you an aging schedule plus an existing allowance balance, and the adjusting entry is the difference between them, not the computed total.

terms.definition: The sum of a project's future cash flows discounted back to today's dollars, minus its initial cost — positive means the project earns more than the required return.
terms.whyItMatters: Capital-investment items ask whether to buy the equipment, and the sign of this figure is the answer regardless of how large the raw cash flows look.

terms.definition: The result that a distributed data store can hold at most two of three guarantees — consistency, availability, and tolerance of a network partition. Because a partition is a fact of networks rather than a design option, the live choice is only between the other two: refuse the read and stay correct, or answer it and risk handing back stale data.
terms.whyItMatters: Asked why a cloud inventory system showed two stores different stock counts during an outage, the competitor has to name the trade-off the vendor chose instead of calling it a bug.

terms.definition: Requires verifiable parental consent before an operator collects personal information online from a child under 13, along with a clear privacy notice, a parent's right to review and delete what was collected, a ban on conditioning participation on handing over more data than needed, and reasonable retention limits. It binds sites directed at children and general-audience sites with actual knowledge of an under-13 user, and the FTC enforces it with civil penalties per violation.
terms.whyItMatters: A promotion roleplay for a children's product asks whether a sweepstakes entry form may collect email addresses at all.

terms.definition: Four-quadrant triage that sorts a task list on two separate axes, urgency and importance: important and urgent is handled now, important and not urgent is scheduled and is where career-building work lives, urgent and not important is delegated, and neither is dropped. The insight is that a loud task can rank last.
terms.whyItMatters: A management roleplay handed a full inbox and one afternoon is scored on the quadrant each item lands in and the action that quadrant dictates.

terms.definition: A detail file holding one account per customer, vendor, or asset, whose balances must total exactly to the single control account carrying that category in the general ledger — the general ledger holds the summary figure that reaches the statements, this holds the per-name detail that supports it.
terms.whyItMatters: A roleplay asking which specific customers owe the overdue balance is answered from this ledger; the trial balance shows only one combined receivable line.

terms.definition: Investing a fixed amount on a fixed schedule regardless of price, which buys more shares when prices are low and lowers the average cost per share over time.
terms.whyItMatters: Investment roleplays ask how a client should handle a volatile market, and this is the answer that beats trying to time an entry point.

terms.definition: Keep three copies of the data on two different media types with one copy held off-site; the arithmetic is the whole point, because a single fire cannot reach the off-site copy, a single failing drive model cannot corrupt the second medium, and one ransomware blast radius cannot encrypt all three at once.
terms.whyItMatters: A storage roleplay about a flooded back office is graded on stating the counts, since answering 'we back up nightly' does not survive the follow-up about where the backup was sitting.

terms.definition: Sworn statement the CEO and CFO sign with every quarterly and annual report, affirming that it is accurate and that they evaluated the effectiveness of disclosure controls as of the period's end. Section 906 supplies the teeth: a knowing false certification carries fines up to $5 million and imprisonment up to 20 years.
terms.whyItMatters: An accounting roleplay about pressure to delay recognizing an expense is answered by naming who personally signs for the numbers and what the penalty is.

terms.definition: Scores difficulty against a fixed list of roughly 3,000 words a fourth-grader is known to recognize: 0.1579 x (percent of words absent from the list) + 0.0496 x (average sentence length), plus 3.6365 whenever more than 5 percent of the words are unfamiliar. It is the only common formula that can call a short word hard because it is rare, so 'writ' counts against the score and 'refrigerator' does not.
terms.whyItMatters: A question asking why a two-syllable legal term makes a customer notice harder to read than a five-syllable everyday word is answered by the familiar-word list, not by syllable counting.

terms.definition: Recording a bad debt only when one specific account is judged worthless, charging it to expense in that later period — required on U.S. tax returns but unacceptable under GAAP for material amounts, because it breaks the match between the expense and the revenue that created the receivable, which the allowance method preserves.
terms.whyItMatters: Exam items ask why a small firm's books disagree with its tax return, and the timing split between these two methods is the reason.

terms.definition: The percentage used to convert a future dollar into today's dollars; raising it lowers the present value of every future cash flow and can flip a project from worth doing to not.
terms.whyItMatters: It is the input that makes a net-present-value question answerable, and exam items test that a riskier project carries a higher one.

terms.definition: Striping with parity distributed across at least 3 disks: usable capacity is (n−1)/n of the raw total, so four 2 TB disks give 6 TB rather than 8, and exactly one disk may fail with no data lost. The exposure is the rebuild — a second failure while the array reconstructs the first destroys everything on it.
terms.whyItMatters: A storage-purchase roleplay asks how much of a quoted 8 TB array the business actually gets and how many drive failures it survives; both numbers come straight from the level.

terms.definition: Allocation of professional growth into three ratios: 70% from challenging on-the-job assignments, 20% from developmental relationships such as coaching and feedback, and only 10% from formal courses. It reframes a development plan away from a training catalog and toward the stretch assignment that produces most of the learning.
terms.whyItMatters: A roleplay building a development plan for a high-potential employee loses points if the whole plan is a list of seminars.

terms.definition: Cost minus salvage value, divided by total estimated lifetime output, multiplied by the units actually produced this period — expense tracks usage rather than the passage of time, so a machine that sat idle all year records none at all.
terms.whyItMatters: Given a press rated for 500,000 impressions and 40,000 run this year, the exam expects the per-unit rate, not the straight-line annual amount.

terms.definition: A privacy demand the business must first authenticate as coming from the consumer, then answer within 45 days, extendable once by a further 45 with notice, covering the categories collected in the preceding 12 months. It must be handled free of charge unless it is manifestly unfounded or excessive, and acting on it without verifying identity is itself a breach.
terms.whyItMatters: A roleplay where a caller demands their records deleted tests whether the competitor verifies identity before acting and can state the response clock.

terms.definition: The yearly percentage of assets a fund charges to operate, deducted from returns automatically so the investor never sees a bill for it.
terms.whyItMatters: Comparing two funds with identical holdings in an investment scenario comes down to this figure, since it compounds against the client every year.

terms.definition: Mirrored pairs that are then striped: usable capacity is exactly half the raw total, so the same four 2 TB disks give 4 TB instead of 6, but the array survives one failure in every pair and rebuilds by copying a single disk rather than recomputing parity from all the rest.
terms.whyItMatters: Comparing two quotes for the same four drives, the competitor has to trade 2 TB of capacity against a faster, safer rebuild — a judge expects the capacity figure said out loud.

terms.definition: Worker excluded from federal overtime because the job clears both a salary-basis test and a duties test — at least $684 a week, which annualizes to $35,568, plus genuine executive, administrative or professional duties. A non-exempt worker, salaried or not, earns 1.5 times the regular rate beyond 40 hours in a week, and a job title alone never settles the classification.
terms.whyItMatters: An exam item on worker rights that gives an assistant manager a $700 weekly salary and 50 hours is testing both prongs of this test at once.

terms.definition: Cash the company has already recorded and sent to the bank that the bank has not yet posted, so it is ADDED to the bank side of a reconciliation — the opposite column from an outstanding check, which is also unposted by the bank but subtracted there, and neither one requires a journal entry on the books.
terms.whyItMatters: Reconciliation items are scored on which column they adjust and whether an entry is needed, and this pair is the one candidates reverse most often.

terms.definition: The nominal return minus the inflation rate — what an investment actually gained in purchasing power, which can be negative while the account balance rises.
terms.whyItMatters: Exam items pair a 2% savings account with 3% inflation and ask whether the saver gained; the account grew and the money bought less.

terms.definition: Sum of the market shares of the four biggest sellers: 18 + 15 + 9 + 6 = 48%. Crossing roughly 40% marks an industry as an oligopoly, and 100% is a monopoly or a tight cartel — but because it adds shares without squaring them, it cannot tell four equal firms apart from one giant and three minnows.
terms.whyItMatters: Competition questions give a share table and ask for the structure label plus its threshold, and the blind spot is exactly what the follow-up tests.

terms.definition: Written with dollar signs as $A$1, it pins both the column and the row so the address does not shift when the formula is copied down or across; a relative reference such as A1 moves with the copy, and a mixed reference such as $A1 or A$1 freezes only the half carrying the dollar sign.
terms.whyItMatters: Spreadsheet items give a tax rate in one cell and ask why copying the formula produced zeros further down the column; the missing dollar signs are the graded answer.

terms.definition: Inventory of the behaviors a role requires, each rated on a defined proficiency scale — commonly five levels from awareness to expert — with written behavioral anchors describing what each level looks like in practice. A job description lists duties and reporting lines; this states how well, which is what makes it scoreable.
terms.whyItMatters: A roleplay asked to justify why one of two equally experienced candidates is ready for the role needs a scored scale, not an impression.

terms.definition: The depreciation schedule the Internal Revenue Code requires on tax returns, assigning each asset class a fixed recovery period and IRS table percentage under a half-year or mid-quarter convention — deliberately faster than the straight-line figure the same asset carries on the GAAP books, which is exactly what creates a deferred tax liability.
terms.whyItMatters: Questions asking why book income and taxable income differ for the same delivery truck are answered by naming this schedule and its accelerated front-loading.

terms.definition: The total annualized return on a bond held to the end of its term, counting coupon payments plus any gain or loss between purchase price and face value.
terms.whyItMatters: A bond bought below face value returns more than its stated coupon rate, and this is the figure that shows it in an investment comparison.

terms.definition: The bit count of a cryptographic key, which cannot be compared across algorithm families: a 256-bit symmetric key doubles in strength with each added bit, while a 2048-bit RSA key rests on the difficulty of factoring and rates at only about 112 bits of equivalent strength. The far bigger number is the weaker key.
terms.whyItMatters: A vendor-security roleplay asks whether a supplier advertising 2048-bit encryption beats one advertising 256-bit; reading the digits alone gives the wrong recommendation.

terms.definition: Ownership raises valuation: in the classic mug experiments sellers demanded roughly twice what buyers would pay for the identical item, minutes after the mugs were handed out at random. Ordinary supply and demand predicts no such gap, and loss aversion supplies the mechanism -- giving up what you hold is coded as a loss rather than as forgone gain, which is also why a free trial and a trade-in allowance both move the price a buyer accepts.
terms.whyItMatters: In a negotiation roleplay, letting the other side describe the arrangement as theirs before you ask them to change it costs you money; the tested application is sequencing the concession before the sense of ownership forms.

terms.definition: Warning an employer must send before rejecting an applicant because of a background-check report, enclosing a copy of the report and a summary of rights under the Fair Credit Reporting Act, then waiting a reasonable interval — five business days is the common practice — so the applicant can dispute an error before the final adverse-action notice issues.
terms.whyItMatters: A hiring roleplay where a screening report shows a charge that belongs to someone else is scored on this two-notice sequence and the gap between them.

terms.definition: A permanent write-down under ASC 360: when events suggest a long-lived asset will not recover its carrying amount, that amount is first compared with the undiscounted future cash flows the asset will generate, and only if it fails that recoverability test is it written down to fair value — a one-time loss, not the periodic allocation depreciation performs.
terms.whyItMatters: Roleplay scenarios about a shuttered plant still carried at cost test whether you know the write-down is required rather than optional.

terms.definition: What a sum invested today grows to by a stated date at a stated rate, computed forward with compounding rather than by adding equal yearly amounts.
terms.whyItMatters: Savings-goal items give a monthly deposit and a rate and ask what the account holds in ten years; straight multiplication understates it.

terms.definition: Two different inputs producing the same fixed-length digest, which has to be possible because inputs are unlimited and digests are not. A 256-bit digest has 2^256 possible outputs, but the birthday bound puts an attacker's expected work at about 2^128 attempts — the square root, not the full space — which is why a 128-bit digest is retired and a 256-bit one is not.
terms.whyItMatters: An information-ethics item asks why a system that stores digests instead of files can still be attacked; the square-root shortcut, not the digest length on the label, is the reasoning.

terms.definition: Promise of company shares delivered on a vesting date and taxed as ordinary income on the full market value at vest — 400 shares vesting at $50 is $20,000 of W-2 wages whether or not a single share is sold. A stock option instead taxes the spread at exercise and is worth nothing while the price sits below the strike, which this grant never is.
terms.whyItMatters: Comparing two offers in a roleplay is impossible without valuing the equity: the exam wants shares times price times the vesting fraction, plus the tax hit at vest.

terms.definition: A structured conversation held with a current, valued employee while there is still time to act, asking what would make them leave and what keeps them — the findings can change that person's situation. An exit interview asks similar questions after the resignation is submitted, so its value is only aggregate trend data for future employees; the timing is the whole difference between the two.
terms.whyItMatters: A retention roleplay that proposes only exit interviews concedes every departure; judges look for the forward-looking conversation with people still on the payroll.

terms.definition: A company's own shares bought back and held rather than retired, carried at repurchase cost as a NEGATIVE item within stockholders' equity and never as an asset. It draws no dividend and casts no vote, which is precisely why issued shares and outstanding shares stop being the same number once a buyback occurs.
terms.whyItMatters: Earnings-per-share questions require the outstanding share count, and a buyback is the event that pulls the two counts apart.

terms.definition: The exposure of a bondholder to rate changes: when market rates rise, existing bonds paying the older lower rate fall in price, and longer maturities fall further.
terms.whyItMatters: It is why an investment roleplay calls long-term bonds risky for a client who may need the money early, despite the bonds being fully repaid at maturity.

terms.definition: A primary key spread across two or more columns, where uniqueness is broken only when every column in the key matches at once — a key on (student_id, course_id) lets the same student appear 6 times and the same course appear 300 times, but the pair exactly once.
terms.whyItMatters: Enrollment and order-line questions ask how many rows one student or one product may hold; the count comes from reading the columns in the key, not from any rule about the table.

terms.definition: Subtraction run one competency at a time — required proficiency minus current proficiency — with the resulting gaps ranked by size multiplied by how critical the competency is, so a 2-point gap on a critical skill outranks a 3-point gap on a peripheral one. Without the criticality weighting it degenerates into a list of everything someone cannot do.
terms.whyItMatters: An exam item on assessing your own interests and skills against an employer's expectations is really asking for this weighted subtraction.

terms.definition: The excess of a purchase price over the fair value of the identifiable net assets acquired in a business combination — recognizable only through an acquisition, never for internally built reputation — and under ASC 350 never amortized, only tested for impairment at least annually.
terms.whyItMatters: Balance-sheet questions following an acquisition ask what the large intangible line actually represents and why it does not depreciate like equipment.

terms.definition: A brand's share of category advertising spend minus its share of category sales — 12% of spend against 8% of sales gives +4 points. Binet and Field's analysis of IPA effectiveness cases found roughly every 10 points of positive excess buys about half a point of annual market-share growth, so a brand that holds its budget flat while rivals raise theirs loses share on an unchanged budget because the metric is relative, not absolute.
terms.whyItMatters: Budget roleplays that propose holding advertising spend steady are answered with this relative measure, which shows why a flat budget is a cut in competitive terms.

terms.definition: A contract paying a fixed stream of income for a set term or for life, bought with a lump sum — insurance against outliving savings rather than an investment for growth.
terms.whyItMatters: Retirement roleplays raise it for a client who fears running out of money, and its trade-off is giving up access to the principal.

terms.definition: A precomputed lookup of billions of password-to-digest pairs that reverses an unprotected stored password in seconds. Adding a distinct random value to each record before hashing defeats it by arithmetic rather than by secrecy: the attacker must now build one table per record, so 1,000,000 stored passwords demand 1,000,000 tables instead of the single shared one.
terms.whyItMatters: Asked why one breached company's passwords were readable overnight and another's were not, the competitor has to explain the per-record work multiplier, not just say the second one 'used encryption'.

terms.definition: Pay increase tied to a published price index rather than to performance — Social Security's 2.5% raise for 2025 came directly from the CPI-W. Relocation uses the same arithmetic: moving a $60,000 salary to a city with a cost index of 130 against a base of 100 takes $78,000 to hold the same purchasing power.
terms.whyItMatters: A roleplay weighing a transfer offer to a more expensive city is scored on running the index ratio, not on comparing the two base salaries.

terms.definition: An outlay charged to expense in the period incurred because it only maintains an asset's existing capacity — routine repairs, servicing, replacement parts — as opposed to a capital expenditure, which extends useful life or output and is therefore added to the asset account and depreciated across the years it benefits.
terms.whyItMatters: Exam items hand you an oil-change bill and an engine-rebuild bill on the same truck and ask which one hits this year's income statement in full.

terms.definition: A basket of securities that trades on an exchange throughout the day like a single stock, unlike a mutual fund, which prices once after the market closes.
terms.whyItMatters: Recommending one over a mutual fund in an investing roleplay rests on intraday pricing and typically lower costs, not on different holdings.

terms.definition: A doctrine holding that one bottleneck sets the output of the whole system, worked through five focusing steps — identify the constraint, exploit it, subordinate everything else to it, elevate it with added capacity, then repeat because the constraint has moved — so improvement anywhere else adds inventory, not throughput.
terms.whyItMatters: When a production roleplay describes one slow station, the judge wants the constraint named and the rest of the line paced to it, not a blanket speed-up of every station.

terms.definition: An independent report on whether a service provider's controls actually operated across an observation window, normally 3 to 12 months of collected evidence. A Type I examines the same controls on one single date and attests only that they were designed correctly — so a vendor holding only a Type I has never had those controls tested over time.
terms.whyItMatters: A vendor-selection roleplay puts two cloud providers side by side, one with each report; the observation period is the distinction a judge scores.

terms.definition: Development instrument that collects ratings from four vantage points — self, manager, peers and direct reports, usually 8 to 12 raters in total — and reports where the self-rating and everyone else's diverge. A performance appraisal is single-source and administrative, feeding pay and promotion, which is exactly why these results are normally kept out of it.
terms.whyItMatters: A roleplay on using development resources is scored on knowing this tool informs growth, and that folding it into a pay decision makes raters stop being honest.

terms.definition: The private, non-governmental body that writes U.S. GAAP and publishes it as the Accounting Standards Codification, operating under SEC oversight rather than by direct statute — distinct from the International Accounting Standards Board, which issues IFRS for most of the rest of the world.
terms.whyItMatters: Regulation questions ask who actually sets the rules a U.S. company must follow, and the answer is a standard-setting board, not a government agency.

terms.definition: The percentage of a covered cost the policyholder keeps paying after the deductible is met, such as 20% of every bill until an out-of-pocket maximum is reached.
terms.whyItMatters: Health-plan comparison items test that meeting the deductible does not end the client's share of the bill.

terms.definition: Combines two tables and keeps only the rows matching on the join column, silently discarding unmatched rows from both sides — 500 customers joined to an orders table returns nothing at all for the 120 who have never ordered, so a customer count taken after the join reports 380 rather than 500.
terms.whyItMatters: A data-analysis item asks why a mailing list built from a joined query is short by exactly the number of inactive customers; the join type is the entire answer.

terms.definition: A goal system pairing one qualitative objective with three to five numeric key results scored 0.0 to 1.0, where roughly 0.7 is the intended landing point for stretch goals; unlike a KPI, which monitors an ongoing business rate, each key result is a quarter-long target that expires.
terms.whyItMatters: Written management events ask you to convert a vague team aim into measurable targets, and the graders look for the numeric key results and the scoring interpretation.

terms.definition: Earnings measured in what they buy rather than in dollars received: a 3% raise against 4% inflation is a cut of roughly 1%, since 1.03 divided by 1.04 comes to 0.99. The nominal number on the offer letter can rise every single year while this one falls, which is why a raise is judged against the inflation rate and not against last year's salary.
terms.whyItMatters: An exam item giving a raise percentage and an inflation rate is asking for this comparison, and the trap answer is the one that calls any raise an improvement.

terms.definition: A postponement entry for cash that has already changed hands but has not yet been earned or used up — unearned revenue and prepaid assets sit on the balance sheet until the service is delivered or the benefit consumed — the exact reverse of an accrual, where the revenue or expense is recognized first and the cash follows later.
terms.whyItMatters: Adjusting-entry questions are sorted by deciding which side of this split a transaction falls on before any journal entry gets written.

terms.definition: The amount a policyholder pays out of pocket before insurance pays anything, and the lever that moves premiums — a higher one lowers the monthly cost and raises the risk carried.
terms.whyItMatters: Insurance-selection scenarios ask which policy suits a client, and the answer depends on whether they could absorb that first payment in an emergency.

terms.definition: A state privacy law binding a for-profit business only once it crosses one of three thresholds: more than $25 million in annual gross revenue, personal information on 100,000 or more California consumers or households, or at least 50% of revenue earned from selling or sharing that information. A small firm holding California data can sit entirely outside it.
terms.whyItMatters: A legal-issues item asks whether a startup with 4,000 California customers and $2 million in revenue must honor deletion requests; only the thresholds answer it.

terms.definition: Written 30-, 60- or 90-day document listing measurable targets, the support the employer will provide and the stated consequence of missing them. It is not progressive discipline's verbal-then-written-warning ladder: discipline addresses conduct the employee chose, this addresses capability, and it doubles as the documentation trail for a for-cause termination.
terms.whyItMatters: A supervision roleplay about an employee who is trying hard and still missing quota calls for this, while a no-call-no-show calls for the discipline ladder instead.

terms.definition: A court's power over the defendant rather than over the dispute, established by presence, domicile, consent, or the minimum-contacts standard from International Shoe, under which the defendant purposefully availed itself of the forum state and the claim arises from those contacts. Subject-matter jurisdiction is the separate question of whether the court may hear that kind of case at all — federal diversity jurisdiction, for example, demands complete diversity plus more than $75,000 in controversy.
terms.whyItMatters: Judicial-system exam items ask where an online seller can be dragged into court after shipping into another state.

terms.definition: A fund fixed at a set dollar amount where every disbursement must be backed by a receipt, so vouchers plus remaining cash always equal that fixed total and replenishment is written for exactly what was spent — unlike a fluctuating fund, topped up in round sums, where a shortage simply disappears into the next refill.
terms.whyItMatters: Cash-control roleplays ask how a small office can hand out cash all week and still detect a missing twenty dollars; the fixed balance is what makes the shortage visible.

terms.definition: Federal law requiring lenders to disclose the annual percentage rate, finance charge and total payments in a standard form before a consumer signs.
terms.whyItMatters: It is why two loan offers in a roleplay can be compared at all, and why a lender quoting only a monthly payment is out of compliance.

terms.definition: The legally fixed span between learning of a personal-data breach and having to report it — 72 hours to the supervising authority under EU rules, with U.S. state statutes commonly allowing 30 to 60 days for notice to the individuals affected. The clock starts at awareness, not at the intrusion, so an attack that sat undetected for 8 months still leaves the full window intact once it is found.
terms.whyItMatters: An incident roleplay asks when the company is late; competitors who count from the intrusion date report the firm as months overdue when it is in fact on day one.

terms.definition: Seven-factor analysis the Department of Labor applies to decide whether an unpaid intern is really an employee: who gains the greater benefit, whether the work is tied to academic credit, whether it displaces paid staff, and whether either side expects a paid job at the end. If the employer is the main beneficiary, minimum wage and overtime are owed retroactively.
terms.whyItMatters: An entrepreneurship roleplay staffing a startup with unpaid interns is scored on this test, because failing it turns free labor into back wages.

terms.definition: A potential obligation that depends on some future event — a pending lawsuit, a warranty claim, a loan guarantee. Under ASC 450 it is accrued as both expense and liability only when the loss is probable AND reasonably estimable; when it is merely reasonably possible it is disclosed in the notes and stays off the balance sheet entirely.
terms.whyItMatters: Exam items describe a suit filed in November and ask whether it changes the statements or only the footnotes, and the two-condition test decides it.

terms.definition: Hofstede's third national-culture score, on a 0 to 100 scale, for how far a society rewards competition, achievement and visible success over cooperation, modesty and quality of life. A high score predicts that public recognition and a stretch target motivate a sales force; a low score predicts that consensus and protected time off do, and that an assertive closing style reads as rude. Japan scores about 95, Sweden about 5.
terms.whyItMatters: An international-business roleplay that asks you to design an incentive plan for sales teams in two countries is judged on changing the reward itself, and this is the dimension that tells you which reward lands.

terms.definition: A deposit locked for a fixed term at a fixed rate, paying more than a savings account in exchange for a penalty on early withdrawal.
terms.whyItMatters: Savings-vehicle scenarios rule it out for an emergency fund precisely because the money is not reachable without giving up interest.

terms.definition: Pairs every row of one table with every row of another under no condition at all, so the output is m × n rows — 50 products against 12 months yields 600. A two-table query whose join condition is left off collapses into one, which is how a query over 1,000 and 2,000 rows returns 2,000,000 and freezes the report.
terms.whyItMatters: A troubleshooting item shows a report that suddenly returns millions of rows from two small tables; the multiplication, not the data, explains it.

terms.definition: Minimum number of members who must be present for a body's votes to count — a majority of the membership under Robert's Rules unless the bylaws set something lower, often one third. Business conducted without one is void rather than merely defeated, so a motion that loses 3 to 2 stands as rejected while the same motion passed short of this number stands as nothing at all.
terms.whyItMatters: A chapter-officer or board roleplay in which half the members skip the meeting is scored on whether the competitor recognizes that no decision can be made.

terms.definition: The IASB-issued reporting framework used across most non-U.S. markets. It is principles-based where U.S. GAAP is rules-based, bans LIFO outright, permits upward revaluation of fixed assets to fair value, and allows reversal of a prior inventory write-down — three things GAAP forbids.
terms.whyItMatters: Questions about a firm that reports in two markets test whether you can name a specific divergence rather than just assert that the frameworks differ.

terms.definition: Federal law governing consumer credit files: it grants access to the report, sets who may pull it, and obliges a bureau to investigate a disputed item.
terms.whyItMatters: A client in a roleplay whose report shows an account they never opened has a statutory remedy under it, not just a complaint.

terms.definition: Under the Electronic Fund Transfer Act's implementing rule, a consumer has 60 days from the statement showing a disputed debit-card or ACH transfer to notify the bank; the bank then has 10 business days to investigate, or may extend to 45 calendar days only if it posts provisional credit inside those 10 days, and must report its findings within 3 business days of finishing. Liability for a lost card is capped at $50 when reported within 2 business days of discovery and $500 after that. Credit-card charges are excluded — those run on the Fair Credit Billing Act's two-billing-cycle track.
terms.whyItMatters: A financial-services or banking roleplay in which a client's debit card was drained overnight is scored on whether the competitor cites the 10-business-day investigation and the provisional-credit condition, instead of promising an immediate refund no associate can authorize.

terms.definition: The 128-bit addressing scheme succeeding the 32-bit scheme the internet was built on. Because each added bit doubles the space, 128 bits is not four times larger but 2^96 times larger — the older scheme's roughly 4.3 billion addresses ran out, and the newer one is written as eight hexadecimal groups rather than four decimal ones.
terms.whyItMatters: An item on the scope of the internet asks why address exhaustion forced a change instead of an expansion; the doubling, not the label, is the explanation.

terms.definition: Senior advocate who spends political capital on someone's behalf in rooms that person is not in, putting their name into promotion and staffing decisions and absorbing reputational risk if it goes badly. A mentor spends time instead of capital — advice given directly to you, with nothing of the mentor's own staked on the outcome.
terms.whyItMatters: A roleplay on advancement patterns is scored on this distinction, because the competitor who only asks for coffee chats never gets named in the promotion meeting.

terms.definition: Tax that will come due in later years because a temporary timing difference — most often faster depreciation on the return than on the books — held taxable income below book income now. It reverses in future periods, unlike a permanent difference such as a government fine, which never reverses and creates no such account.
terms.whyItMatters: Balance-sheet questions ask why a profitable firm reports a tax obligation far larger than the check it actually wrote to the IRS this year.

terms.definition: Charging interest above the legal ceiling a state sets, which makes the loan itself unlawful rather than merely expensive.
terms.whyItMatters: It is the legal line separating a high-cost lender from an illegal one in consumer-credit scenarios, and the reason rate caps exist at all.

terms.definition: A 32-bit pattern splitting an address into a network part and a host part: a /24 leaves 8 bits for hosts, which is 2^8 = 256 addresses, of which 254 are assignable once the network and broadcast addresses come out. A /25 halves that to 126 usable, so borrowing a single bit costs half the room on the segment.
terms.whyItMatters: Asked how many devices a store's network segment can hold, the competitor must convert the slash number into host bits and then subtract 2 — the raw power of two is the wrong answer.

terms.definition: (Price − marginal cost) ÷ price, running from 0 under perfect competition to near 1 for an unchallenged monopolist. A $50 price on $40 of marginal cost scores 0.20, and because the figure equals the reciprocal of demand elasticity, a firm facing elasticity of 5 can hold only a 20% markup over marginal cost.
terms.whyItMatters: Pricing-power items ask how much a firm can charge above its own marginal cost, and the elasticity link converts a demand estimate into a markup ceiling.

terms.definition: Prompt demanding a specific past incident, on the premise that past behavior predicts future behavior, with answers scored against written anchors — which is why a hypothetical answer earns zero. A situational question does the opposite, asking what you would do in a scenario you have never faced, and is scored for reasoning rather than evidence.
terms.whyItMatters: The interview portion of a job-seeking roleplay is graded on giving a dated, quantified incident when the question asks for one, not a description of your general habits.

terms.definition: The portion of a stock issuance received above the arbitrary par amount — shares sold at $12 with a $1 par put $1 per share into the common stock account and the other $11 per share here — so only the two accounts read together show what investors actually contributed.
terms.whyItMatters: Equity-section questions give an issue price and a par value and expect the proceeds split correctly across both lines rather than dumped into one.

terms.definition: Money held by a neutral third party until an obligation is met — in a mortgage, the monthly share of property taxes and insurance the lender collects and pays out.
terms.whyItMatters: It explains why a mortgage payment exceeds principal and interest in a home-buying scenario, and why it changes when taxes are reassessed.

terms.definition: Hits divided by total lookups — 900 of 1,000 is 90%. Read as percentage points the figure misleads: moving from 90% to 95% cuts the 100 misses that reach the database down to 50, so a five-point gain halves backend load, and the last few points are worth far more than the first.
terms.whyItMatters: A technology-impact item asks whether a small improvement to a caching layer is worth the spend; the answer runs on misses removed, not on the headline percentage.

terms.definition: Cover document sent with an application to a posted opening, naming the requisition and tying two or three of its stated requirements to specific evidence from your record. A letter of inquiry does the same job for a company with no advertised opening, so it opens with the employer's problem instead of with a listing.
terms.whyItMatters: A written-event or job-search roleplay that supplies a job posting expects the letter to answer that posting's requirements point by point.

terms.definition: Overestimating how visible one's internal state is to other people. Speakers certain their nervousness was obvious are rated no more nervous than calm speakers by the audience, and people telling a lie believe they are being read far more than they are. The error concerns inner states specifically -- nerves, doubt, irritation -- which is what separates it from the parallel mistake about outward appearance and conduct.
terms.whyItMatters: A competitor convinced the judge can see their hands shaking starts apologizing for nerves that were never detected, spending scoring time on damage control; the counter is to keep delivering the presentation as planned because the leak is far smaller than it feels.

terms.definition: The oversight body created by the Sarbanes-Oxley Act to register, inspect, and discipline the firms that audit public companies and to set the standards those audits follow — replacing the profession's earlier self-regulation through the AICPA, which now writes standards only for private-company engagements.
terms.whyItMatters: Ethics and regulation questions ask what structurally changed for auditors after the accounting scandals, and the end of self-policing is the specific answer.

terms.definition: A court-supervised liquidation discharging most unsecured debts by selling non-exempt assets, unlike a Chapter 13 filing, which keeps assets under a multi-year repayment plan.
terms.whyItMatters: Debt-control scenarios test that student loans and most taxes survive discharge, and that the filing sits on a credit report for a decade.

terms.definition: The 1,024-based unit an operating system counts in, set against the 1,000-based unit a drive is sold in: a '1 TB' disk holds 10^12 bytes, but the OS divides by 1,024 three times and reports 931 GB — a 7% shortfall that widens at every prefix step, so a 4 TB drive shows as 3.64 TB, roughly 9% short.
terms.whyItMatters: A records-storage item asks how many years of files a purchased drive really holds; sizing the archive off the number on the box overstates capacity before the first backup runs.

terms.definition: The information return a business files for every non-employee it paid $600 or more for services in a calendar year, furnished to both the worker and the IRS by January 31. Nothing is withheld, so the contractor carries the whole 15.3% self-employment tax (12.4% Social Security + 2.9% Medicare) and pays it in quarterly estimates, whereas a Form W-2 employee splits that load with an employer paying 7.65%; a payee who supplies no taxpayer ID triggers 24% backup withholding.
terms.whyItMatters: Career-cluster exam items ask what changes when a firm hires a freelance designer instead of a staff one, and a professional-development roleplay where the judge plays a first-time gig worker is graded on naming the $600 filing trigger and the fact that no tax comes out of the check.

terms.definition: Something that happens between the balance-sheet date and the day statements are issued. ASC 855 splits them in two: if the underlying condition already existed at the balance-sheet date — a customer bankruptcy confirming a receivable was already bad — the statements are adjusted; if the condition arose afterward, such as a warehouse fire in January, it is disclosed only.
terms.whyItMatters: Year-end roleplays ask whether a January development changes December's reported numbers, and this recognized-versus-nonrecognized split is the whole answer.

terms.definition: The deadline for bringing a federal discrimination charge — 180 calendar days from the discriminatory act, extended to 300 days in a deferral state that has its own fair employment agency covering the same conduct. Filing the charge is a prerequisite to suit, and once the agency issues a right-to-sue notice the employee has 90 days to file in court, a separate and much shorter clock.
terms.whyItMatters: Complaint-handling roleplays test whether you know an internal investigation does not pause the statutory clock, and the 180/300-day split is the point being probed.

terms.definition: The bureau's file of a consumer's accounts, balances and payment history — the underlying record, not the three-digit number calculated from it.
terms.whyItMatters: A client disputing a score in a roleplay has to correct the report first, since the score is only a summary of what the report says.

terms.definition: A spreadsheet address locking exactly one of the two coordinates — $B5 pins the column and lets the row travel, B$5 does the reverse. Filling a multiplication grid both across and down needs one of each inside the same formula ($B5*C$4); pinning both coordinates or neither returns a wrong value in every cell except the one it was typed into.
terms.whyItMatters: Spreadsheet items grade the filled grid rather than the first cell, so a formula that is correct where it is written and wrong everywhere it is dragged scores zero.

terms.definition: Software that parses every application into structured fields and ranks candidates by keyword match against the requisition before a recruiter reads a single one. Multi-column layouts, text inside images and invented section headings are dropped during parsing, so a qualified candidate can be screened out by formatting rather than by qualifications.
terms.whyItMatters: A job-search roleplay advising a competitor whose applications get no response usually turns on this filter, not on the strength of the experience.

terms.definition: The threshold at which an omission or misstatement would change a reasonable user's decision.
